6.0.s.en: (1) The obligations of the Nazirite during his vow

6.0.0.en: Separate themselves: to be set apart and distinguished by special conduct and behavior from the rest of the congregation.

6.0.1.en: God defined for Moses the duties of the person, man or woman, for there is no spiritual difference between them, who offers himself as a vow to the Lord. The Nazirite was either by the choice of the Lord, like Samson and John the Baptist, or a person vowed his son, like Samuel, or a person vowed himself to the Lord for a period of time, which the Talmud says is not less than a month, like Paul the Apostle. The spiritual concept of the Nazirite is that he withdraws from the pleasures of the world, lives as an ascetic and devotes himself entirely to the service of God, and it is an optional law for whoever wishes.

6.1.0.en: Vine tree: the grapevine or grape tree.

6.1.1.en: Kernels: the seed of the grape.

6.1.2.en: Wine: the product of the vine is meant.

6.1.3.en: Strong drink: old (aged) wine, or one in which the proportion of alcohol has increased so that it became stronger in effect.

6.1.4.en: Vinegar of wine or of strong drink: wine, if exposed to certain weather conditions, may spoil and its taste become close to vinegar, but it does not lose its effect ... and the poor used to drink this vinegar because of its cheap price. The first obligation that the Nazirite takes on is not to go near wine and everything connected with it at all. For wine points to the joys of the world and the lusts of the flesh, and whoever is consecrated must therefore wean his heart from the pleasures and lusts of the world; and this is the state in which every Christian ought to be, for we died to the world by Baptism and became consecrated, that is, Nazirites for Christ. The prohibition also came upon moist grapes, that is, fresh, or raisins, that is, dried grapes, although they are natural fruit, but because they are the source from which wine comes, God forbade them to the Nazirite, as a clear reference to the spiritual man: it is not enough that a person not sin, but he must also keep away from the sources of evil or sin.

6.1.5.en: To convey this concept God adds in His speech to Moses that the Nazirite must also not eat of the vine itself, that is, the fruit of the grape or its seed.

6.1.6.en: Let us notice together how careful God is of those consecrated to Him and who love His holy name, for He keeps them from approaching the roots or origins of evil, because God who formed us knows perfectly that we are all under warfare and liable to be influenced and enticed ... So flee, beloved, from everything that hinders the salvation of your soul.

6.2.0.en: The second obligation on the Nazirite was that he should not shave his hair throughout the period of his vow, as a clear sign before everyone that he is consecrated and set apart for the Lord during the period of his vow. Since cutting the hair was a sign of a man's adornment, letting the hair grow comes as a sign of self-denial and of not caring about personal appearance.

6.3.0.en: The third obligation is not to touch a dead person, because it is a symbol of touching sin and its consequences, as came in (ch. 5:2), and this includes even close relatives such as father and mother, brothers and sisters ... This obligation also includes not entering the tent of the deceased and not taking part in escorting his funeral. The meaning intended, as with the prohibition of wine, is to keep away from everything connected with sin.

6.3.1.en: Because the consecration of his God is upon his head: that is, his loosened hair is a testimony and sign of his total consecration to God. So he must not forget that.

6.4.0.en: The consecrated person must remain on guard like this throughout the period of his vow and not forget that he is holy, that is, set apart for the Lord, and that this vow has obligations by which he must live ... The subject includes us also, for the Myron with which we were anointed has made us a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, that is, we were set apart for God, and for this reason we must be on guard and keep away from evil and the appearance of evil, even if its source is those nearest to us, so there is no laxity or flattery toward sin at all.

6.5.0.en: Verses (9-12) speak about the remedy required of the Nazirite if he becomes defiled accidentally and without intention. If someone dies suddenly by him in his tent, without previous signs of death, so that he was not on guard and did not keep away, he becomes unclean, and so does his vow, "the head of his consecration," and he must complete the law of purification on the seventh day, which applies to everyone who touched a dead person, except that he must shave the hair of his head, as an indication that the previous days of his vow are not counted.

6.6.0.en: Although his uncleanness came as an accidental thing, God obligated him to come to the priest the day after shaving his hair, that is, on the eighth day, with two young pigeons or two turtledoves, which are the cheapest sacrifices, so that the priest offers one of the two as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering, because without shedding of blood there is no forgiveness for the sin of his uncleanness and the breaking of his vow. The burnt offering is a sweet savor and the appeasing of God, and thus his unintentional sin is pardoned.

6.6.1.en: And shall hallow his head that same day: that is, he becomes ready to let his hair grow again and to begin his vow from the beginning on that eighth day.

6.7.0.en: A lamb of the first year: a lamb one year old.

6.7.1.en: The days in which he was defiled because of the dead all fall away from his vow, and he must begin his vow anew, and on the first day of renewing his vow he brings a lamb one year old and offers it as a trespass offering on the first day of his new vow ... It is known that the trespass offering was offered for sins done unwittingly by a person, and after this offering God accepts his new vow from him.

6.7.2.en: May we learn two important things from the law of the Nazirite: the first is to flee from sin so that we are sheltered from its consequences, and the other is the necessity of apologizing to God and to people for our accidental or unwitting errors, for this teaches us humility on the one hand and comforts the hearts of those we have wronged on the other.

6.8.s.en: (2) What happens when the vow is fulfilled

6.8.0.en: When the days of the vow are fulfilled, the Nazirite comes before God and the priest at the door of the Tent and offers to God an offering, "his offering," which includes more than one thing:

6.8.1.en: First: a burnt offering, that is, one burned entirely on the outer altar, of which no one eats because it is a sweet savor to the Lord, and this sacrifice is a male lamb one year old.

6.8.2.en: Second: a ewe lamb, also one year old, offered as a sin offering for the unwitting sins and the sins of the Nazirite.

6.8.3.en: Third: he also offers "a ram," that is, a sheep, with no age required for it, as a thank offering to God for accepting the vow and for the Nazirite's completing his full period.

6.8.4.en: Fourth: the sacrifices are accompanied by a basket of cakes of unleavened bread well kneaded "mingled," but not leavened, and with the cakes other unleavened wafers anointed, that is, smeared with oil.

6.8.5.en: Fifth: with their meat offering and their drink offerings: it was customary and known that burnt offerings and peace offerings were accompanied by other offerings and drink offerings such as oil and wine (Num 15:1-7). One may refer to the interpretation of these sacrifices and offerings in what came in the interpretation of the Book of Leviticus.

6.9.0.en: The priest begins by offering the sin offering and its detailed rite in (Lev 4:27-35), then the burnt offering as came in (Lev 1, 2), and likewise the peace offering (Lev 3). As for the basket of unleavened bread, he would take one of them, that is, one cake and one wafer, to be burned on the altar also, while the rest of the basket is the portion of the priests, and the same applies to the oil and the wine: a part of it was poured on the altar and the priests kept another part.

6.10.0.en: The head of his separation: his head, on which he let the hair grow and hang loose.

6.10.1.en: The loosened hair was the visible sign of the vow, and for this reason at the end of the period of the vow the Nazirite had to shave his hair and throw the hair into the fire of the altar to consume it. God linked the burning of the hair with the peace offering (the thank offering) as evidence of the Lord's acceptance of the vow and His approval and the delight of His heart in it.

6.11.0.en: Wave them: the priest makes the Nazirite move his hands in the four directions and then raise them upward and lower them downward, for he offers his sacrifice to God who is in every place and dwells in heaven and has mercy on and blesses His children on earth.

6.11.1.en: After the peace offering is boiled, the priest takes the right front leg, called the shoulder of the heave offering, with a cake and a wafer from the basket of unleavened bread, and makes the Nazirite hold them after he has shaved his hair, and the priest holds the Nazirite's hand that grasps what was mentioned and waves them before God, that is, these offerings are presented before the face of God. Everything the Nazirite waves before God is God's portion, so it is given to the priests, who are themselves the portion of the Lord. As a sign of the end of the vow the Nazirite drinks wine, which had been forbidden to him throughout the period of his vow, and thus he returns to his normal life.

6.12.0.en: This verse comes as the conclusion of everything that came in the law of the Nazirite up to the end of the time of his vow.

6.12.1.en: Beside that that his hand shall get: that is, the other things and offerings that he may have vowed to God, which are apart from and in addition to the essential sacrifices and offerings that came in the Law.

6.12.2.en: The Nazirite must fulfill all that he said and pronounced in his vow, for everything he vowed is regarded as a covenant that came out of him and must be fulfilled.

6.12.3.en: The idea of the offering has become absent from many of us. Despite the abundant good that God gives His children, they often turn away from the offering or, at best, offer nothing but tithes ... Although God reminds us not to appear before Him empty (Deut 16:16), we forget that we have brothers in Christ who are in need while bread is abundant with us. So remember that God has rights over you, and remember also that everything you offer with joy gladdens the heart of God as well.

6.13.0.en: The discourse moves to another subject, and God directs His speech to Moses and through him to the priests, "Aaron and his sons," that they must bless the people. This puts before us another work of the priesthood besides offering sacrifices, which is intercession for the people: the priest conveys the offerings and petitions of his people to God and conveys the blessing of God to his people. The blessing was recited with the priest turning toward the people and raising his hands upward above the level of the people's heads, as a sign that graces and blessing have God Himself as their source.

6.14.0.en: The blessing had the following text and content:

6.14.1.en: (1) Blessing and keeping: that is, the priest asks God for spiritual and material blessings for His people, and asks also for His care, shepherding and guarding of His people from anything or any harm.

6.14.2.en: (2) Light and mercy: he also asks that God enlighten the mind of His people so that they are filled with all understanding, guidance, knowledge, insight and spiritual wisdom, and have mercy on their weakness and accept their repentance of their sins.

6.14.3.en: (3) Lift up His countenance: that is, God looks with a special look on His people, the look of a father on his children, and the look of very special care like the shepherd whose eyes do not neglect his sheep.

6.14.4.en: (4) Give His peace: for God is the King of peace and its only source, and it is a peace that includes the mind (thought), the heart (feelings) and the whole life of man.

6.14.5.en: The repetition of the name of the Lord three times in the three verses is to affirm that the source of all blessings is God alone, the Three Hypostases, and none other.

6.15.0.en: By this blessing with which the priests bless the people, they make the name of God exalted and holy always in the hearts and minds of the children of Israel, and likewise God answers the petitions and prayers of the priests for the people, so that the people themselves feel the effectiveness of these requests through God's blessing on them and on their possessions and their whole life.

6.15.1.en: It is good that you enjoy the blessing of the priests and ask for their prayers for you, for they hold the greatest thing in existence, the Body and Blood of the Lord. So kissing their hands and asking for their prayers pours out upon you blessings from God whom they serve.

6.15.2.en: The offering of gifts and sacrifices to the house of the Lord

7.0.s.en: (1) The offering of the wagons and oxen and their distribution

7.0.0.en: Anointed it: that is, poured on it and anointed it with the holy oil (Ex 30:31). Sanctified it: that is, set it apart and consecrated it for the service of the Lord.

7.0.1.en: The vessels thereof: the implements and appurtenances of the service.

7.0.2.en: This verse comes as an introduction to the whole chapter, making clear that the events that follow took place after Moses the prophet finished setting up the tent of meeting and anointing it and consecrating it with all its contents to the Lord.

7.1.1.en: Covered wagons: carts to keep the implements of the tent of meeting when journeying, and they were covered to protect what was in them from rain and sun.

7.1.2.en: The princes of the tribes came, the same ones who numbered and counted all the people (ch. 1), and offered their gifts and offerings before the Lord "before the tabernacle." These offerings consisted of twelve oxen to draw the wagons, one ox for each tribe, with every two oxen sharing in drawing a wagon, and also "six covered wagons," that is, every two tribes share in one wagon.

7.2.0.en: God's command to Moses was that he accept these offerings from the princes of the tribes, and He also charged him to use them in the service, especially at the time of journeying. Since the Levites were the ones charged with this service, Moses distributed them to them with wisdom and according to need, to each group according to the kind of their service.

7.3.0.en: The distribution was as follows: Moses the prophet gave two wagons with four oxen to draw them to the sons of Gershon, since their service, as mentioned in (ch. 4:21-28), was the curtains and coverings of the Tent and the inner pins and cords.

7.4.0.en: As for the sons of Merari, whose work and burdens were heavier, Moses gave them four wagons drawn by eight oxen, since they had to carry the boards of wood, the pillars, the bars, the metal sockets and the outer pins and their cords (ch. 4:29, 30).

7.5.0.en: But the sons of Kohath did not take any of the wagons or oxen, because their loads were the lightest and all of them were carried on the shoulders, and they include the contents of the sanctuary and the Holy of Holies.

7.5.1.en: My beloved brother, there was divine wisdom in the distribution of the wagons and oxen, for the offerings were distributed according to need. As an application to our spiritual life, never compare yourself with others in their gifts or talents and say to yourself, why did the Lord not give me this or that? ... Accept your talents and trade with them, and do not look around you, and trust in the wisdom of God ... for you will be asked only for what you were given, so be careful to be faithful in it.

7.6.0.en: Dedication: setting apart and consecrating for the service of God.

7.6.1.en: The altar: what is meant is the tent of meeting with the bronze altar and the altar of incense it contains and everything in it. Each prince of the tribes of the people came to the Tent after the anointing and sanctifying, offering his offerings and gifts of wagons and oxen and other gifts, as we shall learn, but God's command to Moses was that they should not all come forward on one day, but that a day be assigned to each prince of a tribe on which to offer his offerings. In this way the celebrations of the dedication of the altar continued for twelve days, which were regarded as feasts in their gladness. The expression dedication of the altar does not mean that the dedication was repeated every day, but the celebrations of the dedication are meant.

7.7.0.en: The tribe of Judah and its prince Nahshon the son of Amminadab was the first to offer his offerings, that is, his gifts, on the first day, and the following is noted regarding the order of the days of the offerings:

7.7.1.en: 1- Presenting the offerings was in the order of the places of encampment around the Tent and for no other consideration, so that there would be no competition or quarrel over who should offer his offerings first. Perhaps he began with the tribe of Judah because from it Christ would come (Gen 49:8-12).

7.7.2.en: 2- It mentioned that Nahshon was of the tribe of Judah and not the prince of Judah, although he was a prince, to teach us that leadership is a position for the service of God and not for pride or for controlling others; then in the rest of the tribes it mentioned that the one who offered the offerings was the prince of the tribe.

7.7.3.en: 3- This order proceeded in one direction: the first three tribes were encamped on the east side, the next three tribes were encamped on the south side, and so the tribes of the west side, and finally the north side.

7.7.4.en: 4- The offering of all the princes of the tribes was alike and exactly identical, so explaining the offering of one tribe spares us repetition in explaining the rest of the tribes and their offerings.

7.8.0.en: The details of the offering that the tribe of Judah and its prince presented, and which all the tribes repeated, were as follows:

7.8.1.en: 1- A broad, flat dish of silver weighing one hundred and thirty shekels, that is, about 1.950 kilograms of silver (the shekel = 15 grams).

7.8.2.en: 2- One silver bowl: a deeper dish (hollow) weighing about one kilogram of silver.

7.8.3.en: Both the dish and the bowl were filled with fine flour mingled with oil, to be offered as came in the Book of Leviticus (ch. 2).

7.8.4.en: 3- One golden spoon: its weight was about 150 grams, and sweet incense was offered on it.

7.8.5.en: 4- A burnt offering: this sacrifice consisted of one young bullock, one ram and one lamb of the first year. The difference between the ram and the lamb of the first year is a difference in the age of the two: the ram is the male of the sheep with fully grown horns and is known as the stud of the flock, while the lamb of the first year is a lamb one year of age, that is, ripe for eating but smaller in size and age. All of this was burned on the altar of burnt offering (see Lev 1).

7.8.6.en: 5- A sin offering: it was of a male goat, offered for the sins or unwitting errors in which the prince of the tribe may have sinned, and the priest takes a part of it.

7.8.7.en: 6- A peace offering: this consisted of two oxen, five rams, five he-goats (male goats) and five lambs, each of the first year. These are offerings from which the priests take a portion, and so does the one who offers them, according to what came in the laws of the Book of Leviticus.

7.9.0.en: The same offerings as before were repeated with each tribe, mentioning the name of the prince of the fathers of each tribe before mentioning his offerings or the offerings of his tribe.

7.10.0.en: As for these verses, before the end of the chapter, they came as a summary of all the previous offerings, but in a collective form.

7.10.1.en: The tally was twelve dishes and bowls of silver, the total of their weights being two thousand four hundred shekels, which is equivalent to 36 kilograms of silver.

7.10.2.en: Likewise the total of the golden spoons was twelve spoons weighing one hundred and twenty shekels, which is close to 1.8 kilograms of gold.

7.10.3.en: Likewise the total of the oxen was counted and came to twelve oxen, the total of the rams came to twelve rams, and the total of the he-goats came to twelve he-goats. All of these were offered as sin offerings.

7.10.4.en: As for what was offered as peace offerings, the total number was twenty-four oxen, sixty rams, sixty he-goats, and the lambs of the first year were also sixty.

7.10.5.en: Perhaps the purpose of this final summary of all the offerings is that God wished us to know that nothing is forgotten before Him, but everything we offer Him of vows and offerings is a lasting memorial for us before Him, for God in His justice and love never forgets the labor of love of His children.
